blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define economies and diseconomies of scale, explain why average cost per unit falls as a firm grows larger and why it may rise again, and read both from a firm's figures.

blocks.heading: Average cost and scale
blocks.text: A firm's average cost is the cost of producing one unit: the whole cost of production divided by the number of units produced. Economies of scale are the falls in average cost that come as a firm grows larger. Diseconomies of scale are the rises in average cost that may return when a firm grows beyond the size its management can coordinate. Both are named for scale because both are about size: what happens to the cost of one unit as the firm's size changes.

blocks.heading: Oshakati Textiles reads its own figures
blocks.text: Oshakati Textiles grew by opening a second production line: output rose from 1 000 to 2 000 shirts a month and average cost fell from N$40 to N$34 a shirt. The savings come from being a bigger firm. Ordering twice the cotton earns a bulk-buying discount. A firm this size can justify a specialised cutting machine that a small output could not keep busy. Banks tend to lend to a larger firm more cheaply, and it can afford a specialist production manager. This differs from spreading the same rent over more units without growing, which lowers average fixed cost and belongs to topic 3.7. A Brazilian steel works gains the same way, buying iron ore by the shipload at a lower price per tonne.

blocks.heading: Too large to coordinate
blocks.text: The fall has limits. Past some size, average cost starts rising again, and the mechanisms are the reverse of the ones that brought it down. Coordinating departments takes meetings and reports, and in a firm of many layers a decision that once took a morning takes a week. Messages travel through more people on the way from the top to the line, so instructions arrive late or changed. Workers in a very large firm may feel like a small part of a big process, and effort and care tend to fall with that feeling. Where growth came by merger the strain is sharper still: two sets of managers and habits must be made into one.

blocks.heading: Internal and external economies of scale
blocks.text: The savings at Oshakati Textiles are internal economies of scale: they come from the firm's own growth. External economies of scale are falls in a firm's average cost that come from the growth of its whole industry in an area, whatever the firm's own size. As fish processing has grown around Walvis Bay, firms there can hire workers already trained in filleting and cold storage; specialist suppliers of nets, ice and packaging have set up nearby, as have engineering firms that repair boats and refrigeration units; the port and the roads serving it have been improved; and training courses for the industry are run locally. A new processor that opens there with 20 workers gains these savings at once, although it is small. In Switzerland's Jura region, watchmakers have long gained in the same way from a pool of skilled craftworkers and specialist parts makers.

blocks.heading: External diseconomies, and what scale does to an industry
blocks.text: The growth of an industry in one area can also raise costs. External diseconomies of scale are rises in a firm's average cost caused by the growth of its industry in an area: roads and port berths become congested, so deliveries take longer; firms compete for land, so rents rise; firms compete for the same skilled workers, so wages are bid up; and water and electricity supplies may be stretched. These raise the costs of the firms across that area, including firms that have not grown at all. Internal and external effects therefore act on different scales. Internal economies and diseconomies change one firm's average cost as that firm grows. External economies and diseconomies change the average costs of the firms across an industry as the industry grows in an area. While an industry is growing from a small base, external economies tend to win, and the industry's costs fall, which may let its firms charge lower prices and compete abroad; as it crowds into one place, external diseconomies tend to take over, and some firms may move to a new area.
